stories.title: Rammohun Roy and the Abolition of Sati
stories.description: Rammohun Roy, an 18th-century Bengali reformer, campaigned against sati (widow burning) not through force but through intellectual engagement. He showed how sati contradicted Hindu scriptures and philosophy. Through persuasion and appealing to people's existing values, he succeeded.
stories.insight: The most durable social change comes through persuasion that engages people's reasoning, not coercion. Reformers who help people see contradictions in their own beliefs are more effective than revolutionaries.
stories.why_share_worthy: Demonstrates how one person with conviction, rhetoric, and appeal to values can shift entire societies. Relevant to modern social change.

stories.title: Aligning Reform With Economic Interest
stories.description: Sustainable reforms often succeed because they align with people's material interests. A landowner might oppose a policy until they realize they'd benefit economically. Smart reformers find the intersection of morality and self-interest.
stories.insight: Durable change isn't just moral; it's economically sensible too. Reformers succeed when they show how change benefits people materially.
stories.why_share_worthy: Reveals the practical psychology of how real change happens, not just how it should happen.

recommendations.title: Historical Works on Rammohun Roy and Indian Reformers
recommendations.author: Various historians
recommendations.why: Understanding figures like Rammohun Roy provides insight into how societies evolve through persuasion and reform rather than revolution.

core_ideas.title: The Power of Persuasion: How Real Change Happens
core_ideas.description: Reformers succeed by engaging reason and appealing to values people already hold. Rammohun Roy didn't ban sati; he showed Hindus that sati violated their own principles. Change that engages intellect lasts.
core_ideas.why_matters: Suggests that lasting social change comes through reasoning, not force. Laws imposed without changed minds don't persist.

core_ideas.title: Radical vs. Gradualist Approaches to Reform
core_ideas.description: Some reformers push for sudden, complete change (radical); others work incrementally (gradualist). Radicals may achieve more visibility but risk backlash; gradualists make steady progress but may accept too little.
core_ideas.why_matters: Different contexts call for different approaches. Understanding both helps evaluate reform strategies.

core_ideas.title: The Reformer's Dilemma: Inside vs. Outside Power
core_ideas.description: Reformers must choose: work within institutions (limited but achievable) or work outside to delegitimize them (risky but potentially transformative). Both paths have costs.
core_ideas.why_matters: Explains why reformers compromise and why others are radical. There's legitimately no perfect answer.

jokes_and_cultural_references.quote: A reformer changes not what people do, but what they believe about what they do.
jokes_and_cultural_references.author: Implied from discussion
jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Rammohun Roy persuaded rather than forced, changing beliefs more than laws
jokes_and_cultural_references.why_funny_and_insightful: Captures the essence of how lasting social change actually happens
